outline.description: Sets the stage with the parties, facts giving rise to the dispute, the district court’s Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, and the appellate lens through which the Second Circuit reviewed the case.
subtopics: Parties and platform: George Santos; Jimmy Kimmel; ABC and Disney; Cameo and JKL
Factual setup: Kimmel used fictitious names to order Santos Cameo videos; aired them in JKL segments titled “Will Santos Say It?”
Claims asserted: federal copyright infringement; state claims for breach of contract, breach of implied contract, and fraudulent inducement
District court ruling: dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6); fair use bars copyright claims; state claims preempted or otherwise deficient
Standard of review: de novo review of dismissal
Materials considered on 12(b)(6): complaint, exhibits, incorporated materials, and judicial notice of Copyright Office registrations

outline.chapter_title: Fair Use Framework and the Transformative Purpose Inquiry
outline.description: Explains the statutory fair use factors, the centrality of transformative purpose, the ability to resolve fair use at the pleading stage, and applies those concepts to Kimmel’s use of the videos.
subtopics: Fair use statute and factors: 17 U.S.C. § 107’s non-exclusive list and flexible application
Pleading-stage fair use: when allegations can establish the defense on a motion to dismiss
Transformative use focus: whether the secondary use adds new purpose or character (reasonable observer standard)
Application to this case: JKL’s purpose was commentary on Santos’s willingness to say absurd things for money
Rejection of Santos’s “instigator/designer” argument: subjective intent of either party does not control the purpose inquiry
Bad faith/deception argument: limited role after Harper & Row; no allegation that defendants sought to supplant Santos’s market; use motivated by criticism/commentary
First-factor bottom line: strongly favors fair use

outline.chapter_title: The Remaining Fair Use Factors and Overall Balance
outline.description: Covers the court’s analysis of the nature of the works, amount/substantiality, and market effect, and explains why the balance justified dismissal on fair use grounds.
subtopics: Nature of the works: published status supports fair use and reduces weight of the second factor
Amount and substantiality: challenges to the district court’s analysis rejected
Market effect: focus on substitution/usurpation, not harm from criticism; no competing substitute here
Licensing markets: unlikelihood that creators license criticism or lampoons removes such uses from potential markets
Scope of the record: only the original videos and the JKL segments needed to decide fair use
Overall conclusion: fair use established on the face of the complaint; copyright claims dismissed at 12(b)(6)

outline.chapter_title: Contract-Based State Claims: Terms of Service and Implied Agreement
outline.description: Addresses why the court bypassed preemption and found the contract theories legally insufficient under governing state law.
subtopics: Preemption posture: court affirms on failure-to-state-a-claim grounds without resolving preemption
Breach of Cameo Terms of Service: Santos not a party to the TOS that users accept
Illinois third-party beneficiary law: strong presumption against conferring enforceable rights; need an implication practically equivalent to an express declaration
Absence of express third-party beneficiary language for the provisions Santos invokes; contrast with other TOS provisions that do include such language
Implied-in-fact contract under New York law: need to plead essential terms and a meeting of the minds
Pleading defects: no nonconclusory essential terms; no plausible allegation that Kimmel agreed to adhere to the TOS or otherwise undertook definite obligations to Santos

outline.description: Explains the failure of the fraud claim for lack of out-of-pocket loss, and summarizes the court’s affirmance and practical implications.
subtopics: New York fraud damages: out-of-pocket rule requires actual pecuniary loss
Application: Santos alleged no actual out-of-pocket loss from the alleged deception
Result: fraudulent inducement claim dismissed
Final disposition: judgment affirming dismissal of all claims

Practical takeaways: satire/commentary can be fair use even if content was procured deceptively; criticism does not usurp markets; platform TOS are generally not enforceable by nonparties; fraud requires concrete pecuniary damages
